---
title: "Determinism"
---

Jestyr's central promise: the same source produces the same bits, on every run
and on every supported platform. Not "usually the same." The same.

This page states the contract precisely, shows how each piece is enforced, and
gives the commands that prove it. Scope is stated with every claim — determinism
here is verified on Windows + gcc (MinGW/msvcrt) and Ubuntu 24.04 + gcc 13.3
(glibc). macOS/clang is untested.

::: {.claim}
**One digest, two operating systems, two libcs.** The determinism canary — a
program exercising the entire numeric stack — hashes to
`4389bf83…` on Windows 11 + MinGW gcc and on Ubuntu 24.04 + gcc 13.3.0.
CI re-checks the digest on every push. macOS/clang is untested.
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle</span>
:::

## Why determinism is hard for a language that emits C

Jestyr compiles to C and builds it with gcc. That means the language does not
inherently control floating-point behavior:

- `a*b+c` can fuse into an FMA, which rounds once instead of twice — a
  different result on hardware that fuses versus hardware that doesn't;
- `-ffast-math` would license reassociation, so `(a+b)+c` and `a+(b+c)` become
  interchangeable — and they are not the same value in floating point;
- libc's `printf("%g")` formats floats differently across implementations, so
  even a correct computation can *print* differently;
- parallel reductions sum partial results in whatever order threads finish.

Any one of these breaks bit-identical output. The contract closes all of them,
at compile time where possible, by construction where flags can't reach.

## Part 1: locked compile flags

Every translation unit `jestyrc` builds gets the same flags:

```bash
-O2 -std=c11 -ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math
```

`-ffp-contract=off` forbids FMA fusion. `-fno-fast-math` forbids reassociation
and other value-changing "optimizations." The flag set is asserted by a test
(`fp_determinism_flags_are_locked`) that fails if anyone removes a flag, so the
invariant is part of the test suite, not a convention.

**Scope:** the flags ride the `jestyrc` build path. If you `emit-c` and compile
the output yourself without them, the guarantee does not follow you. x86-64
(SSE) is the verified target; legacy 32-bit x87 extended precision is
unaddressed.

## Part 2: deterministic by construction

Flags stop the compiler from changing your arithmetic. The standard library
goes further: its numeric primitives are designed so that evaluation order
cannot matter in the first place.

- **`parse_float`** — Eisel–Lemire fast path plus a division-free big-integer
  slow path. Correctly rounded for *any* digit count, not just the easy cases.
- **`format_float`** — Dragon4 shortest round-trip, correctly rounded,
  locale-free. Jestyr programs never need libc's `%g`, so output formatting is
  identical everywhere by construction.
- **Binned superaccumulator** — sums floats into integer exponent bins with
  add-time carry and a correctly-rounded finalize. The result is invariant to
  chunk size and thread count because the accumulation is exact until the final
  rounding.
- **`par_binned_sum`** — a parallel reduction that is bit-identical to its
  serial counterpart, built on the superaccumulator. The escape checker forbids
  `mut`-slice spawn parameters, so the safe subset is race-free by rule, not by
  review.

Each primitive carries property tests (`proptests::lemire`,
`proptests::dragon`, `core_props::binned_*`) in the 916-test default suite.

## Part 3: the compiler rejects non-determinism

Determinism is not just a library discipline — the type system enforces it.

**`@deterministic` certifies schedule independence.** Inside a
`@deterministic` function, the raw concurrency primitives whose results can
depend on the thread schedule — `concurrent`/`spawn` and the `atomic_*`
operations — are compile errors. The only parallelism allowed is the checked
deterministic reduction:

```{.rust}
@deterministic fn sum_of_squares(read s: []i64) -> i64 {
    return par for x in s reduce(core.sum_reduction()) { x * x }
}
```

**`par for … reduce(r)` accepts only declared-deterministic reduction
constructors.** A reduction whose result depends on combination order (say,
non-associative float addition folded pairwise in thread-completion order) is
rejected at compile time. You cannot accidentally write a parallel loop whose
answer varies run to run.

**`@span` makes parallel depth a checked part of the signature.** Declare
`@span(log)` on a parallel reduction and `@span(linear)` on its serial
reference:

```{.rust}
@span(log)    fn par_sum(read s: []i64)    -> i64 { ... }
@span(linear) fn serial_sum(read s: []i64) -> i64 { ... }
```

If a refactor quietly serializes the `par for` into a `for`, the declared
`@span(log)` no longer holds and the compiler names the cause. Performance
shape is part of the contract, not a comment.

## The proof: a purified SHA-256 canary

Claims need a falsifier. Jestyr's is a single dedicated program,
`examples/std/numerics_canary.jtr`, that exercises the whole numeric stack —
bit primitives, serial and parallel reductions, the binned superaccumulator,
parse and format — through the real `jestyrc run` pipeline. Its complete output
is hashed with a dependency-free, self-tested SHA-256, and the digest is locked
in the test suite:

```
4389bf8328ae7e018ebf0fb6ca4f94dd95f65eb7fb24568e55b1170b809868bc
```

Three properties make this canary trustworthy:

1. **Purified output.** The demo prints only integers and `format_float`
   strings — nothing through `printf("%g")`. So a digest mismatch can *only*
   mean a genuine determinism break, never a libc formatting difference. Float
   results are pinned by their formatted value, not by pass/fail flags, so the
   canary stays sensitive to single-ULP drift.
2. **SIMD lane width is pinned.** The demo carries two `@simd` loops — 8 `i32`
   lanes over 23 elements, leaving a 7-element scalar remainder — and their
   realized values enter the hash. A vector lowering that stopped agreeing with
   the scalar path flips the digest.
3. **Mutation-verified.** Changing a single parsed value in the demo moves the
   digest and trips a companion token assertion. The canary detects what it
   claims to detect.

::: {.claim}
**The digest is re-verified on every push.** CI runs the canary on
Ubuntu 24.04 + gcc 13.3.0 alongside the Windows development runs. Same source,
two OSes, two libcs (msvcrt and glibc), one digest. A mismatch anywhere is
treated as a determinism regression to triage — never a reason to re-lock.
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle</span>
:::

## Demonstration: deterministic concurrency in `pi.jtr`

`examples/pi.jtr` estimates π by Monte Carlo on four threads. Each worker owns
a fixed-seed Lehmer generator; hit counts are accumulated with `atomic_add`
(addition is associative and commutative over integers, so accumulation order
cannot change the total); `concurrent { … }` joins every task at the closing
brace.

```bash
jestyrc run examples/pi.jtr
```

::: {.program-output}
6300
3150
:::

Twenty consecutive runs produce twenty identical outputs: 6300 hits,
π × 1000 = 3150. The threads interleave differently every time; the answer
never does.

**Scoped phrasing, because scope matters:** Jestyr's deterministic concurrency
facilities produce reproducible results across interleavings and platforms
*when per-task state and reduction semantics are deterministic* — fixed seeds,
order-insensitive accumulation, declared-deterministic reductions. Write a
schedule-dependent program with the raw primitives and it will behave like one;
that is exactly what `@deterministic` exists to forbid, function by function,
where you choose to claim it.

## What is and is not claimed

| Claim | Scope | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| Identical canary digest | Windows/MinGW-gcc and Ubuntu 24.04/gcc 13.3; macOS/clang untested | `cargo test --features c-oracle`, CI on every push |
| Flags locked | the `jestyrc` build path only; manual builds of emitted C are on you | `fp_determinism_flags_are_locked` |
| Correctly-rounded parse/format, order-invariant sums | the stdlib primitives, property-tested | default suite (916 tests) |
| Schedule-independent functions | code inside `@deterministic`; raw primitives elsewhere are unchecked by design | compile-time rejection tests |
| `pi.jtr` reproducibility | one program, 20/20 identical runs; the general claim is the scoped phrasing above | `jestyrc run examples/pi.jtr` |

Known open edges, stated plainly: macOS/clang is a welcome third data point,
not yet collected. The emitted C does not yet carry
`#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` in the file itself, so the invariant lives in
the build command rather than the artifact. 32-bit x87 is unaddressed; x86-64
is the verified target.

Next: see the [Tour](tour.qmd) for the language these guarantees attach to, or
[Performance](performance.qmd) for what determinism costs (medians on one
machine: fib(40) at 0.984× hand-C — correctness is cross-platform via CI,
timings are local).
